title: How the LCLS-II DAQ works, from detector to disk
question: At a high level, how does the LCLS-II DAQ work, from detector to disk?
summary:
The LCLS-II DAQ (data acquisition system) records detector data one accelerator pulse at a time. The timing system, whose firmware is outside this repository (the lcls2 repository), triggers groups of detectors and gives every event a pulse ID and a timestamp, the keys that later tie the pieces of an event together ([[timing]]). Besides these per-pulse events, called L1Accepts, the same timing stream carries transitions such as Configure, BeginRun and Enable, with which the control process steps every process through a run ([[control]]).

Each detector readout has its own DRP (data reduction pipeline), which builds an XTC2 datagram, the DAQ's self-describing data record, for every event ([[drp]]). The trigger decision is kept off the data path: the DRPs send only small trigger inputs to the TEB (trigger event builder), and the TEB answers the DRPs with a result saying whether to record the event and whether to monitor it ([[teb]]). Each DRP then writes its own file stream, a big-data `.xtc2` file plus a small-data `.smd.xtc2` index ([[files]]), and sends monitored events to live monitoring, where an MEB (monitoring event builder) puts them together for online analysis ([[monitoring]]). For recording, the DAQ never assembles an event in one place: psana later joins the streams by timestamp ([[after-run]]).

nodes.title: Timing and triggering
nodes.summary: The timing system gives each readout a pulse ID and timestamp, decides which pulses trigger which detectors, and carries transitions.
nodes.prose:
The LCLS-II accelerator timing system, which is outside this repository, sends one timing frame per accelerator bucket. An XPM (eXperiment Partition Master), a timing-system board whose trigger logic is firmware outside this repository ([[xpm]]), turns that stream into triggers: detectors are placed in readout groups, each triggered by one selection, for example an event code.

Every event that a DRP (data reduction pipeline) builds starts from a timing header with the pulse ID and a timestamp. The DRP reads this header from its DMA (direct memory access) buffers ([[pulse-id]]). Data that come without such a header, such as EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) values, are paired with these events. The online event builders match the pieces of one event by pulse ID; after the run, psana builds events again from the recorded files.

The same timing stream also carries transitions such as Configure, BeginRun and Enable. The control process asks the XPM to insert them, so a readout stream holds both transitions and per-pulse L1Accept events, each with its own pulse ID.
nodes.dev_notes: Timing-side code in this repository: `psdaq/psdaq/pyxpm/` (XPM control software) and `psdaq/psdaq/service/EbDgram.hh` (the timing header as seen by a DRP). The control-to-XPM calls are in `DaqXPM` in `psdaq/psdaq/control/control.py`.

decisions.title: Transitions travel through the timing system
decisions.decision: After the software message for a transition, sent over ZeroMQ (a messaging library), has been answered, the control process asks the XPM to insert the transition into the timing stream. Each DRP (data reduction pipeline) then receives the transition in a timing header, in the same DMA (direct memory access) stream as the L1Accepts, and builds its datagram from that header.
decisions.rationale: The internal Two Phase Transitions page describes the split. The first phase is a broadcast so that slow work such as configuring can run in parallel. The second phase, handled by the DRP thread that reads the timing stream, only collects what the first phase prepared. This repository does not show why the second phase rides on the timing stream; one effect is that a transition gets a pulse ID and a timestamp like any event.

code_refs.note: In the PGP reader, a transition arriving from DMA gets an EbDgram built from its timing header, and the XTC prepared in phase 1 is copied in.

nodes.title: Accelerator pulses and event codes
nodes.summary: The accelerator timing stream defines the buckets, event codes and beam destinations that triggers are built from.
nodes.prose:
The accelerator's timing system defines the time grid the DAQ (data acquisition system) works on. The LCLS2 Timing page gives the basic numbers: every 0.98 s holds exactly 910,000 buckets (the time slots of that grid), so a bucket comes about every 1.08 microseconds (about 929 kHz), and the accelerator's timing patterns repeat with the 0.98 s period.

Timing frames carry event codes, which arrive about 100 microseconds before the beam, and beam destinations, for example the SXR (soft X-ray) undulator line or the dump used for dropped shots. Per the same page, timing receivers (the boards and firmware blocks that decode the timing stream) build each trigger from two conditions that must both hold. One is a rate condition: a fixed rate, an AC (alternating-current) power-line rate, or an event code or sequence. The other is a beam-destination condition: don't care, inclusive or exclusive. The page also says that the DAQ readout groups are added to the timing frame as extra bits at its end; [[pulse-id]] shows where a DRP (data reduction pipeline) finds them in the timing header it reads.

nodes.title: XPM: readout groups and triggers
nodes.summary: XPM firmware picks, per readout group, the pulses that trigger a readout and inserts transitions; this repository holds its host software.
nodes.prose:
An XPM (eXperiment Partition Master) is a timing-system board. Detectors are assigned to readout groups, and all detectors of a group share one trigger selection: a fixed rate, an AC (alternating-current) power-line rate, an event code or a sequence. Its FPGA (field-programmable gate array) firmware, kept outside this repository in SLAC's `l2si-core` repository, picks the triggering pulses of each group (the trigger its registers call L0) and inserts transitions into the timing stream.

This repository holds the host software: `pyxpm` maps the board's registers with `pyrogue` (the Python interface of SLAC's Rogue platform) and serves them as EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) process variables (PVs), among them each group's trigger selection and `DstSelect` (the beam destination).

By default, to insert a transition the control process writes the transition ID to the groups' `MsgHeader` PVs and the group mask to `GroupMsgInsert`, and it writes `GroupL0Enable` to switch L0 triggering on. What the board does with these registers is defined in the firmware.

Each group's PVs also include `MsgHeader`, `L0Groups` and `L0Delay`, and `pyxpm` refuses firmware older than a minimum version. The firmware registers behind the PVs include `groupL0Enable` and `groupMsgInsert` (pyrogue `RemoteVariable` entries in `psdaq/psdaq/pyxpm/xpm/_XpmApp.py`). The LCLS2 Timing page describes the sequence engines inside the XPM that generate event codes. Given an XPM host, the control process sends these register writes to that host as ZeroMQ (a messaging library) messages instead of writing PVs (`DaqXPM` in `psdaq/psdaq/control/control.py`).

nodes.title: Pulse ID, timestamp and transitions
nodes.summary: Every readout a DRP receives by DMA carries a timing header: a 56-bit pulse ID, a timestamp, the triggered readout groups and the transition type.
nodes.prose:
Every readout that a DRP (data reduction pipeline) receives in a DMA (direct memory access) buffer carries a timing header, and the detector class tells the DRP where it is. The default `getTimingHeader()` takes the start of the buffer; `BEBDetector`, the base of many hardware detectors, skips one or two event-batcher headers first; and the GPU (graphics processing unit) DRP skips a DMA descriptor.

The header's first 64-bit word holds the pulse ID in the low 56 bits; the upper 8 bits are control bits, whose low 4 bits are the transition ID. Then come a timestamp (32-bit seconds and 32-bit nanoseconds), an `env` word (32 bits; the low 16 are the readout groups triggered for this pulse) and an event counter.

Transition IDs run from 0 to 12: Configure, BeginRun, BeginStep, Enable, SlowUpdate and their counterparts are transitions, and 12 is L1Accept, the per-pulse event.

The online event builders, the TEB (trigger event builder) and the MEB (monitoring event builder), match contributions by pulse ID. psana's `evt.timestamp` is the timestamp packed as (seconds << 32) | nanoseconds.

Contributions are inserted into events keyed by pulse ID.

`BEBDetector` skips the event-batcher header (two of them when debatching) before the timing header.

nodes.title: Detector front-ends and readout links
nodes.summary: For detectors read over PGP links, the electronics (firmware outside this repository) send each triggered readout with a timing header to a DRP node's card.
nodes.prose:
Detector front-ends are the electronics and FPGA (field-programmable gate array) firmware at each detector, outside this repository; one example is the timing-receiver module of the separate `lcls2-pgp-fw-lib` firmware library ([[detector-electronics]]). When the XPM (eXperiment Partition Master) triggers their readout group, detectors with PGP links, the serial readout links of the DAQ (data acquisition system), send the data over them to a readout card in a DRP (data reduction pipeline) node, which the code opens as a device. Data that arrive another way, such as EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) values, are read by their own kinds of DRP and paired with timing headers ([[timing]]).

The card's firmware, also outside this repository, places each readout in a DMA (direct memory access) buffer in host memory, together with the timing header that carries the pulse ID; for some detector classes, such as those built on `BEBDetector`, other headers come first ([[pulse-id]]). The DRP software maps these buffers, reads them and returns them.

code_refs.note: The default `getTimingHeader()` takes the start of the DMA buffer as the timing header; detector classes may override it.
`BEBDetector` overrides it: the timing header follows the event-batcher header(s).
MemPoolCpu: open the device and map its DMA buffers (dmaMapDma).
allocateDma only counts the buffers in use; readDma and freeDma read and return them through the driver.

decisions.title: Timestamp the data in firmware at high rates
decisions.decision: Detectors that run at high rates get their timestamp in firmware, from a timing-receiver firmware module built into the detector's readout FPGA (field-programmable gate array); that firmware is outside this repository. For low-rate standalone detectors the public page on user-supplied detectors describes a second option, also outside this repository: a timing-receiver board (the page calls it a TPR PCIe card) in a computer the users provide. Together with software the users write themselves, the board reads the timestamp and attaches it to their data.
decisions.rationale: The public page on standalone detectors ties the choice to the rate: it gives about 100 Hz as a rule of thumb for the software option and says that at higher rates the timestamping typically has to be done in firmware.

nodes.title: Detector firmware and timing receivers
nodes.summary: Detector readout firmware receives the timing stream, makes the trigger decision in time, and attaches the event's timing information.
nodes.prose:
In the DAQ (data acquisition system), triggering and timestamping at detectors read over PGP links (its serial readout links) are done in FPGA (field-programmable gate array) firmware, outside this repository. The public page on user-supplied standalone detectors names the timing-receiver module of the open-source `lcls2-pgp-fw-lib` firmware library as the interface for triggering within the DAQ. That module takes in the timing fiber and puts out, for each event, the trigger decision in time for the readout, a header for the event and the event's complete timing information; the timing stream runs at 3.71 Gb/s with 8B/10B encoding.

The same page describes two options for detectors outside the DAQ. At lower rates (about 100 Hz as a rule of thumb) a timing receiver board in a PCIe (PCI Express) slot plus user software can timestamp the data; at higher rates the timestamping typically has to be done in firmware with that module.

nodes.title: Readout card and DMA buffers
nodes.summary: The DRP reads completed DMA buffers from the readout card in bulk and returns them when done.
nodes.prose:
On a DRP (data reduction pipeline) node the readout card is a device given with the `drp -d` option, and the PGP lanes to read (the card's serial readout links from the detector) are given as a lane mask, one bit per lane, with `-l`. The DMA (direct memory access) buffers belong to the card's driver and firmware, outside this repository; the DRP maps them with `dmaMapDma()` and counts the ones in use.

The DRP's PGP reader thread calls `dmaReadBulkIndex()` to collect several completed buffers at once, each with a size, a buffer index and a destination word; the buffers are handed back to the driver later. When readouts arrive faster than about 1 kHz the reader polls the driver; at lower rates it waits for an interrupt, and while nothing arrives it backs off exponentially. Readouts from several lanes of one detector are assembled into one event by the [[drp-pgp-reader|PGP reader]].

code_refs.note: drp options: -d device, -l lane mask, -D detector type, -o output directory.

nodes.title: DRP: readout and reduction
nodes.summary: One DRP process per detector readout builds XTC2 datagrams, asks the TEB what to do with each event, and writes its own files.
nodes.prose:
A DRP (data reduction pipeline) is one process per detector readout. It reads the detector's DMA (direct memory access) buffers and uses a detector-specific class to turn each readout into an XTC2 datagram (the DAQ's self-describing data record, [[xtc2-format]]). It also sends a small trigger contribution for every event to the TEB (trigger event builder). The `buildAll` and `buildDets` keys of the trigger configuration can turn this off, but only when `buildAll` is not 1 and the `buildDets` string starts with the DRP's detector name. The TEB answers with a result that says whether to record the event and whether to send it to monitoring.

The DRP then writes the events it records to its own file and posts the monitored ones to the MEB (monitoring event builder). The detector data never go to the TEB: the TEB input of each event is only the datagram header plus the output of a trigger-primitive plugin, compiled code loaded from a shared library that condenses the event into a few bytes for the trigger. All DRPs are driven by the control process through transitions such as Configure, BeginRun and Enable.

code_refs.note: setupTriggerPrimitives: no trigger input (contractor = 0) only when buildAll is not 1 and buildDets starts with the detector name (buildDets.find(detName) is 0); the TEB input size, the EbDgram header plus TriggerPrimitive::size().

decisions.title: Send the TEB a small summary, not the data
decisions.decision: A DRP that provides trigger input sends the TEB only an event header plus a few bytes made by a trigger-primitive plugin loaded from a shared library; the event data stay in the DRP until the result comes back.
decisions.rationale: The internal TEB/MEB page notes that the trigger-input format between the DRP and the TEB can be kept simple because it is never written to disk. It also notes that the input is produced in the DRP by compiled shared-library code, while the decision itself may be written in C++ or Python. This repository does not show why the full data are kept out of the TEB; the TEB input buffers are sized to the header plus `TriggerPrimitive::size()`.

nodes.title: The drp process
nodes.summary: The drp executable parses its options, picks a detector class by name and joins the control protocol.
nodes.prose:
The `drp` executable parses options such as the platform number (`-p`, which identifies the DAQ instance: one control process and the processes it drives) and the output directory (`-o`). It also parses the lane mask (`-l`, one bit per PGP lane, a serial readout link of the readout card), the detector type (`-D`), the collection host (`-C`) and the device (`-d`). Then it creates, initializes and runs a `PGPDetectorApp`. `PGPDetectorApp` derives from `CollectionApp` ([[collection-protocol]]), so the process answers the first steps of the control protocol (rollcall, alloc and connect; see [[control-process]]) and then receives the transitions from the control process.

The `-D` name selects the detector class through `Factory<Detector>`; registered names include `hsd`, `epix100`, `jungfrau`, `opal`, `wave8` and `ts` (the timing system). Other executables use the same base code for other inputs, such as `drp_bld` (beam-line data), `drp_pva` (EPICS PV Access: PV stands for process variable, EPICS for the Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) and `epicsArch`, which records EPICS variables.

nodes.title: Threads and buffers of a DRP
nodes.summary: A reader, several workers, a collector and a result receiver pass events along through fixed buffer pools.
nodes.prose:
Inside a DRP (data reduction pipeline) that reads PGP links, the serial readout links from the detector, the work is split across threads connected by queues. One PGP reader thread collects DMA (direct memory access) buffers, checks the timing headers and groups events into batches. A configurable number of worker threads run the detector code on the batches. One collector thread passes finished events to the TEB (trigger event builder) contributor, and a result receiver handles what the TEB sends back.

Events live in fixed buffer pools. The DRP reads the DMA buffers, returns them to the card's driver and counts them. The pebble, the code's name (`Pebble`) for the large buffer in which the datagrams are built, has one slot per event, and its slots are allocated and freed strictly in order. Transitions have separate buffers. The reader closes a batch when the pulse ID moves into the next block of `batchSize` pulse IDs, when a transition other than SlowUpdate arrives, or when no new data have arrived for a short time-out.

code_refs.note: PGPDrp::startup starts the worker threads, the PGP reader and the collector.
Batch boundaries: a time-out without DMA data, a new block of pulse IDs, or a transition other than SlowUpdate.
The pools of one DRP (declarations): the pebble, the DMA buffer addresses and the transition datagrams.

allocateDma only counts; readDma and freeDma read and return DMA buffers through the driver; allocate hands out pebble slots in order, blocking when all are in use, and freePebble expects them back in that order.

nodes.title: PGP reader: lanes and timing header
nodes.summary: The reader assembles the lanes of each readout into an event using the timing header, and drops events the rest of the system cannot handle.
nodes.prose:
For each DMA (direct memory access) buffer, the PGP reader asks the detector class for the buffer's timing header (`getTimingHeader()`; it is not always at the start of the buffer, see [[pulse-id]]). The header's event counter selects the event slot, and the buffer's lane (one of the PGP links, the readout card's serial links) is marked in that event's lane mask. The event is complete when every lane given with the `-l` option of the DRP (data reduction pipeline) has delivered its buffer. The reader checks that the event counter advances by one; on a jump it logs an error and, for multi-lane detectors, discards incomplete events.

It then drops, and counts, events whose readout groups lack the common readout group (the group whose number is the platform number `-p` of the DAQ instance, see [[teb]]) and SlowUpdate transitions that lack any readout group used in the instance (`rogMask`, taken from the connection parameters). The internal Bypass Events page gives the reason for the first drop: the event builder relies on the common readout group, normally the one with the highest rate, to keep events in time order. Finally it allocates a slot in the pebble (the DRP's large buffer for datagrams) for the event, which can block when all slots are in use.

code_refs.note: Timing header from the detector class, event slot from the event counter, lane mask, completion test and the jump check.
Discard of incomplete multi-lane events after a jump; the common-readout-group filter (rogs & (1 << m_para.partition)); the SlowUpdate filter against rogMask; pebble allocation (m_pool.allocate).

nodes.dev_notes: The drops are counted in `m_nNoComRoG` and `m_nMissingRoGs`.

nodes.title: Workers: building the datagram
nodes.summary: Worker threads build each L1Accept's XTC2 datagram with the detector class and prepare the TEB input.
nodes.prose:
Each worker thread takes batches of events from the reader. For an L1Accept it constructs an `EbDgram` in the event's slot of the pebble (the DRP's large buffer for datagrams) from the timing header that the detector class finds in the event's DMA (direct memory access) buffer. It then calls the detector class's `event()` method, which appends the detector's data as XTC2 containers. When the DRP (data reduction pipeline) runs with Python (`-k drp=python`), the datagram is passed to a Python worker process, and the reply replaces the datagram.

The worker then fills the event's TEB (trigger event builder) input buffer: a copy of the datagram header plus, if a trigger-primitive plugin (compiled code loaded from a shared library, [[teb-trigger-plugin]]) is loaded, the plugin's summary of this event. For a SlowUpdate the detector's `slowupdate()` method fills a transition buffer instead, and the TEB input is just the header.

code_refs.note: workerFunc: the timing header from the detector class, L1Accept and SlowUpdate handling.

nodes.title: Collector: trigger input to the TEB
nodes.summary: The collector frees DMA buffers and hands TEB inputs, batched by pulse ID, to the TEB contributor.
nodes.prose:
The collector thread takes the workers' output batches in the same round-robin order in which the reader handed them out, so events leave it in the order they were read. For each event it returns the DMA (direct memory access) buffers to the driver and hands the event's TEB (trigger event builder) input to the `TebContributor`, the DRP-side sender of TEB inputs.

The contributor groups inputs into batches by pulse ID. It closes a batch when a transition other than SlowUpdate arrives, when the next input falls outside the batch's block of pulse IDs, or when the batch times out while the collector waits for the workers. It also closes a batch when its buffer region wraps around. It queues every batch so that results can be matched to it later. If this DRP (data reduction pipeline) provides trigger input, it also sends the batch over libfabric (the network library under the event builders' links) to one TEB, chosen from the batch's first pulse ID when there are several TEBs.

code_refs.note: PGPDrp::collector: frees the DMA buffers, hands each event to the contributor, and calls timeout() while it waits for the next worker batch.
process(): a batch closes when the region wraps, at a transition other than SlowUpdate (doFlush), or when the pulse ID leaves the batch's block (expired).
_post: every batch goes on the _pending queue; only a batch with trigger input (contractor) is sent, to TEB (pid / maxEntries) % numEbs.

nodes.title: Result receiver: record and monitor
nodes.summary: For each TEB result the receiver records the event if asked, posts it to monitoring if asked, and acknowledges transitions.
nodes.prose:
The result receiver takes the TEB (trigger event builder) results in order and finds the waiting event by its buffer index; it aborts if the pulse ID or transition type of the result and the event disagree. Damage flags from the result (error marks that travel with the data, such as a missing contribution) are added to the event.

While recording, an L1Accept is written to the files if the result's `persist` or `prescale` bit, its two record requests ([[teb-result]]), is set; transitions are always written. An L1Accept is posted to the MEB (monitoring event builder) buffer named in the result if `monitor` is set, and transitions are always posted. For transitions other than SlowUpdate, the receiver also passes the pulse ID on so that it is forwarded to the collection, that is, the control process.

code_refs.note: TebReceiverBase::process: consistency checks and damage.
TebReceiver::complete: write, monitor, acknowledge.

nodes.title: Detector classes
nodes.summary: Each detector type implements one interface: describe the data at Configure, write it for every L1Accept.
nodes.prose:
A detector class implements `Drp::Detector`. Its `configure()` method adds the detector's Configure data to the Configure datagram, and its `event()` method adds each L1Accept's data; hooks for BeginRun, BeginStep, Enable, Disable and SlowUpdate let a detector add data to those transitions. A second `event()` hook receives the TEB (trigger event builder) result for an L1Accept; the DRP (data reduction pipeline) calls it only for the timing-system detector (detector type `ts`), which records the trigger information.

For example, `AreaDetector` (the `fakecam` and `cspad` class) declares `Names` (field names, types and ranks) in `configure()` and writes the event's values against those names in `event()`. Many hardware detectors derive from `BEBDetector`, whose `configure()` calls a Python function `<type>_config` with the configuration alias and turns the returned settings into XTC2 data. A detector class also says where the timing header sits in a readout buffer, through `getTimingHeader()` ([[pulse-id]]).

nodes.title: TEB: trigger decisions
nodes.summary: The TEB gathers the DRPs' small trigger inputs for an event, runs a trigger plugin and tells the DRPs: record it? monitor it?
nodes.prose:
The TEB (trigger event builder) is not on the data path. The DRPs (data reduction pipelines) that provide trigger input send it only a small contribution per event. The TEB builds the contributions for one event, runs a trigger plugin that was loaded from a shared library at Configure, and sends back a result.

The result says whether to record the event (`persist` or `prescale`) and whether to send it to monitoring (`monitor`). Each DRP then records or monitors its own part of the event. For recording, the parts are never merged: each DRP writes its own file.

decisions.title: Every event must include the common readout group
decisions.decision: One readout group, the one whose number equals the platform number (the `-p` number that identifies the DAQ instance), is the common group; normally it is the readout group with the highest rate. Every event the TEB builds must contain it, and DRPs discard events without it before they reach the TEB.
decisions.rationale: The internal Bypass Events page explains that the event builder uses the highest-rate readout group to keep events in time order. Without it, contributions from a slower group could be built and dismissed before an older event arrived. Events would then come out of order, which makes several parts of the system abort. The page also records that an earlier scheme, in which such events bypassed the TEB, caused problems for offline analysis and was given up in favour of dropping these events early in the DRP. At the pinned commit the bypass code is still there: `TebContributor::process` and `EbCtrbInBase` keep a branch that sends such an event past the TEB and marks it to be recorded. This branch is not reached, because the DRP's PGP reader (the thread that reads the detector's links) drops every event without the common readout group before it gets that far. The public operator page states the same requirement on the group number, and the TEB logs an error for a built event that lacks the common readout group.

code_refs.note: The PGP reader drops events without the common readout group and counts them.
The remaining bypass branch on the DRP side (the else of rogs & (1 << _prms.partition)), not reached because of the filter above.

decisions.title: Trigger logic is a plugin named in the configuration
decisions.decision: The TEB contains no trigger logic of its own. At Configure it loads the shared library named by the `soname` key of the trigger configuration and creates the trigger with the library's `create_consumer` function. Each DRP that provides trigger input loads its trigger-primitive producer from the same library. A DRP for a GPU (graphics processing unit) detector loads the library whose name has `_gpu` added before the extension.
decisions.rationale: The internal TEB/MEB page records the view that loading every trigger as a shared library gives one uniform, configurable mechanism, even when the decision logic is written in Python. The public monitoring page shows the Python case: the `soname` is pointed at `libtstTebPy.so` and a Python script is named in the configuration.

nodes.title: The teb process
nodes.summary: The teb executable joins the control protocol, loads the trigger plugin at Configure and runs the event builder.
nodes.prose:
The `teb` executable runs a `TebApp`, which takes part in the control protocol like the DRPs (data reduction pipelines), and a `Teb` event builder. At Configure it receives the trigger configuration from the control process. From it and the connect information it builds, for each readout group, the list of DRPs expected to contribute. It then reads the `soname` key (the file name of a shared library) and loads the trigger plugin from that shared library through its `create_consumer` symbol.

For each built event the `Teb` checks that the pulse ID has advanced: if not, it marks the event with the `OutOfOrder` damage flag (an error mark carried with the data) and aborts, because it cannot recover. It then asks the plugin for the decision, picks a monitoring buffer if one is requested, and posts the result, in batches, back to the DRPs.

code_refs.note: Contributors per readout group, and loading the trigger plugin.

nodes.title: Building contributions by pulse ID
nodes.summary: Contributions with the same pulse ID form one event; an event is complete when every expected DRP has contributed.
nodes.prose:
The event builder of the TEB (trigger event builder), which is shared with the MEB (monitoring event builder), receives batches of contributions from the DRPs (data reduction pipelines) and inserts each contribution into the event with the same pulse ID. When an event is created, its contract, the set of DRPs expected to contribute, is the OR of the contributor lists of the readout groups named in the first contribution.

Events are handed on in pulse ID order once their contract is met. An event can still be missing contributions when it times out, or when a newer complete event with the same expected contributors forces it out. Such an event is fixed up: it gets the `DroppedContribution` damage flag (an error mark in the datagram saying that a contribution is missing). For the first such event, the event builder also sends an error message naming the DRPs it did not hear from.

code_refs.note: process(): each contribution goes into the event with its pulse ID; a complete event becomes due and events up to it are flushed in order.
_flush: an older incomplete event is fixed up when a newer complete event has the same contract; otherwise only after the time-out.
The contract from readout groups, and fix-up of missing contributions.

nodes.title: Trigger plugin: the decision
nodes.summary: A trigger plugin looks at all contributions of an event and fills in the result.
nodes.prose:
A trigger plugin implements `Pds::Trg::Trigger`. The TEB (trigger event builder) calls its `event()` method with the contributions of one built event and a result to fill, for L1Accepts and for transitions.

The example `tmoTeb` plugin reads two values, `persistValue` and `monitorValue`, from the trigger configuration. For each event it sets `persist` if any contribution's `write` field equals `persistValue`, and asks for monitoring by any MEB (monitoring event builder) if any contribution's `monitor` field equals `monitorValue`. On the DRP (data reduction pipeline) side, a `TriggerPrimitive` plugin from the same library produces the contribution fields. The decision can also be written in Python through the `libtstTebPy.so` interface.

code_refs.note: The plugin interface.
A small example plugin and its create_consumer factory.

nodes.title: The result: persist, prescale, monitor
nodes.summary: A result is the event header plus one word of decision bits and one word naming a monitoring buffer.
nodes.prose:
A result is a `ResultDgram`: the event's datagram header followed by a 32-bit result word and a 32-bit monitor-buffer word. In the result word, bit 0 is `prescale`, bit 1 is `persist`, and bits 2 to 5 hold the `monitor` request for up to four MEBs (monitoring event builders). Bits 8 to 31 are an `auxdata` field that a trigger plugin may set; the cube result type, for example, packs a bin number and flags into it.

The trigger plugin sets `persist` and `monitor`; the TEB (trigger event builder) itself sets `prescale` from the event's `keepRaw` flag, bit 22 of the `env` word (the 32-bit header field that also holds the transition ID and the readout groups). The TEB sends each result to the DRPs (data reduction pipelines) that expect results for the event's readout groups, leaving out any expected contributor whose input never arrived. On the timing-system DRP, the result is also passed to the detector class, so that the trigger information is saved with that DRP's data.

The monitor field is MAX_MRQS = MAX_MEBS = 4 bits wide.

nodes.dev_notes: The timing-system (`ts`) configuration sets how often the `keepRaw` bit is set through a `keepRawRate` entry, described as the raw-data retention rate in Hz.

nodes.title: Files on disk
nodes.summary: A run on disk is, per DRP stream, one .smd.xtc2 small-data file plus one or more chunks of .xtc2 big data.
nodes.prose:
Each recording DRP (data reduction pipeline) writes its own files, so a run on disk is a set of streams, one per recording DRP; a DRP selected as monitor-only writes none. A stream has one big-data file per chunk, `<exp>-r<run>-s<stream>-c<chunk>.xtc2`, and a single small-data file, `smalldata/<exp>-r<run>-s<stream>-c000.smd.xtc2`: the small-data file is opened once at BeginRun with the name of the first chunk and stays open when the big-data file moves on to `-c001` and later chunks ([[chunking]]).

The big-data file holds the full datagrams of the recorded events. The small-data file holds a copy of every transition and, for each L1Accept, only its position and size in the current big-data chunk; psana reads the small-data files first and then only the bytes it needs from the big-data files.

decisions.title: One file stream per DRP
decisions.decision: Recorded events are not merged before writing. Each DRP writes the events it records to its own big-data and small-data files, named with its node ID as the stream number, and psana joins the streams later by timestamp.
decisions.rationale: The internal XTC for LCLS-II page states the plan that LCLS-II writes one or more XTC files per detector, in a self-describing format. This repository does not show why events are not merged before writing; only the record/monitor decision is made centrally, by the TEB (trigger event builder), while the data stay in each DRP.

decisions.title: Chunk big-data files at a shared Enable
decisions.decision: A DRP whose big-data file grows past a threshold asks the control process for a Disable/Enable pair. At that Enable, every DRP whose file is past half the threshold starts a new chunk, and the Enable datagram records the new file name. Small-data files are never chunked.
decisions.rationale: The internal Chunking page records a choice between this coordinated scheme and an uncoordinated one in which each DRP would chunk on its own at a SlowUpdate. The coordinated scheme was preferred, in part because the designers did not want a feature that depends on the reliability of deadtime. The internal Live Mode page adds that because the small-data files, which drive psana's live reading, are not chunked, live analysis does not have to deal with chunk boundaries.

code_refs.note: At BeginRun: both files are opened with chunk number c000.
At a new chunk only the big-data file is closed and reopened.
A monitor-only DRP sets run_number to 0 and opens no files; files are opened only when recording.

nodes.title: How a DRP writes its files
nodes.summary: At BeginRun a recording DRP opens its two files; the result receiver writes Configure, the transitions and the accepted events.
nodes.prose:
At BeginRun, if the run has a run number (recording is on), each DRP (data reduction pipeline) not selected as monitor-only creates `<output dir>/<instrument>/<experiment>/xtc/`. It opens `<experiment>-r<run>-s<stream>-c000.xtc2` there, plus the matching `.smd.xtc2` in `xtc/smalldata/`; the stream number is the DRP's node ID. For each file it opens it sends a file report message, with the file's path, host and run number, on toward the control process.

The writing itself happens in the result receiver. When the BeginRun result arrives it first writes the cached Configure datagram and then BeginRun; after that it writes every transition and every L1Accept whose result has `persist` or `prescale` set. At EndRun the files are closed. A detector selected as monitor-only in the partition (the set of processes allocated for the run) is shown in AMI (the online monitoring program) but not recorded.

code_refs.note: Directory layout, file names, file reports.
What is written when.

nodes.title: .xtc2: the big-data file
nodes.summary: The full datagrams, written through a buffered writer with its own writer thread.
nodes.prose:
The big-data file holds complete datagrams, one after another in the XTC2 format. The DRP (data reduction pipeline) writes it through `BufferedFileWriterMT`: `writeEvent()` copies each datagram into one of a pool of page-aligned buffers, and a separate writer thread writes full buffers to the file. A buffer is also queued when the batch in it is more than 2 seconds old by event timestamp.

The writer can open the file with direct I/O (`O_DIRECT`), in which case it uses two large buffers of at least 512 MiB each instead of 64 buffers. When it opens a file it waits for a write lock on it.

code_refs.note: The two buffered writers; the multi-threaded one is used for big data.

nodes.title: .smd.xtc2: the small-data file
nodes.summary: One small datagram per written datagram: transitions in full, L1Accepts reduced to an offset and a size.
nodes.prose:
For every datagram written to the big-data file, the DRP (data reduction pipeline) also writes a small-data datagram made by `Smd::generate()`. Transitions are copied whole (EndRun without payload), and the copy of Configure gains an extra `smdinfo` description with two fields, `intOffset` and `intDgramSize`. Each L1Accept is replaced by a datagram with the same time and `env` word (the header field with the transition ID and readout groups) whose payload is just those two numbers: where the event starts in the current big-data chunk file and how many bytes it has.

The internal XTC for LCLS-II page describes the purpose: each big-data event gets a small-data counterpart, which serves to spread the reading over many processes and, when small values are added, to filter events before the large data are fetched. The Live Mode page notes that it is written by a single-threaded writer.

code_refs.note: addNames and Smd::generate: transitions copied (EndRun without payload, Configure with the smdinfo names intOffset and intDgramSize); an L1Accept becomes those two values.
Each written datagram goes to both files.

nodes.title: Chunking big-data files
nodes.summary: Past a size threshold, the big-data file is closed at an Enable and continued in a new chunk file.
nodes.prose:
While recording, each DRP (data reduction pipeline) counts the bytes in its current big-data chunk. The threshold is 500 GiB (500 × 1024³ bytes, about 537 GB): past it, the DRP's result receiver requests a new chunk, and the control process answers with a Disable followed by an Enable. At any Enable, a DRP whose chunk is past half the threshold advances its chunk number and adds a `chunkinfo` record with the new file name and chunk ID to the Enable datagram.

That Enable is the last datagram of the old chunk; the DRP then closes the big-data file and opens the next one (`-c001`, and so on). The small-data file stays open, and its offsets count from the start of the new chunk.

code_refs.note: Chunk size and the threshold of 500 × 1024³ bytes.

nodes.title: XTC2 datagrams
nodes.summary: Files, network messages and shared memory all carry the same self-describing XTC2 datagrams.
nodes.prose:
XTC2 is the file and network format of the LCLS-II DAQ (data acquisition system); a file or a shared-memory buffer is a sequence of datagrams. Each datagram is one transition or one L1Accept: a header (timestamp and the `env` word with the transition ID and readout groups) followed by a tree of `Xtc` containers.

The data are self-describing. The Configure datagram carries `Names` (field names, types and ranks for every detector and algorithm), and each event carries `ShapesData`, which are decoded with those names. The internal XTC for LCLS-II page lists design goals: the same format in memory and on disk, no copying step to serialize data for the network, and files that can be read while they are being written.

code_refs.note: A datagram: the transition header plus the top-level Xtc.

nodes.title: Fast-feedback file system
nodes.summary: During the experiment the DAQ's files live on the fast-feedback (FFB) file system, where live analysis reads them.
nodes.prose: The DRP (data reduction pipeline) writes into the directory given with its `-o` option. Per the public psana page, analysis while the experiment runs should normally read the data from the fast-feedback (FFB) file system. For the TMO, RIX and MFX instruments the DAQ (data acquisition system) writes its files straight onto the FFB; for UED they are copied there afterwards. (These are LCLS instrument names. Per the LCLS instruments page, TMO stands for time-resolved AMO, and MFX for macromolecular femtosecond crystallography.) The psana page also advises when automatic run-processing jobs should start in each case: at the start of a run for direct writing, and when the first file has been transferred otherwise.

nodes.title: Live monitoring
nodes.summary: Events chosen for monitoring are built by an MEB (monitoring event builder) and served in shared memory to online analysis such as AMI.
nodes.prose:
Live monitoring runs next to recording. Each DRP (data reduction pipeline) posts the events that the TEB (trigger event builder) marked for monitoring to an MEB (monitoring event builder, the `monReqServer` program), which builds the parts from all DRPs into one event and serves it in shared memory. Online analysis, such as AMI and psana scripts in shared-memory mode, reads the events from there.

Monitoring is driven by free buffers. An MEB tells a TEB about each buffer it has free, and an event is only monitored if a buffer is available, so monitoring may see only some of the events. Transitions are sent to every MEB.

code_refs.note: post(dgram, destination): an L1Accept goes to the MEB and buffer that the result names.
post(dgram): a transition is posted on every MEB link.

decisions.title: Monitor an event only when an MEB buffer is free
decisions.decision: An MEB announces each free buffer to a TEB. When the trigger asks for monitoring, the TEB puts one announced buffer number into the result, and each DRP sends its part of the event straight into that MEB buffer. If no buffer is free, the event is not monitored.
decisions.rationale: The public page on distributing events for monitoring explains the scheme. A result has room for only one buffer number. When the trigger lets the event go to any MEB, the TEB cycles through the MEBs in turn and takes a buffer from the first one that can spare one. When none can, the result names no buffer and the event skips monitoring. In the code the TEB cycles through the MEBs only when the monitor request names all of them; otherwise it tries the requested MEBs from the lowest number up. An MEB can spare a buffer only while it holds more free buffers than its reserve (`_rogReserved`), and the TEB option `mon_throttle` makes the TEB skip monitoring for events within that many pulse IDs of the last one it considered. This repository does not show the reasoning behind the design; when no buffer is found the TEB clears the monitor request and still sends the result, so the event can be recorded as usual.

nodes.title: MEB: monitoring event builder
nodes.summary: monReqServer asks the TEBs for events by offering free buffers, then builds the events written into them.
nodes.prose:
The MEB (monitoring event builder) is the `monReqServer` program, and a hutch can run several of them. Its options include the shared-memory tag (`-t`, the name under which clients find its shared memory), the number of event buffers (`-n`) and the number of event queues (`-q`).

Each time the MEB has a free event buffer, it sends that buffer's index to a TEB (trigger event builder), spreading the indices evenly over the TEBs. DRPs (data reduction pipelines) then write the parts of a monitored event directly into the announced buffer over libfabric (the network library under the event builders' links) with RDMA (remote direct memory access: the DRP writes straight into the MEB's memory), while transitions go to every MEB. The MEB builds each event by pulse ID with the same event-building code as the TEB and hands it to its shared-memory server.

code_refs.note: Offer a free buffer index to a TEB (index modulo the number of TEBs).
The DRP side: an L1Accept is posted (link->post) into the MEB buffer named by the result.
link->post is an RDMA write (writedata) into the MEB's memory.
Transitions are posted to every MEB.

nodes.title: Shared memory to analysis clients
nodes.summary: The MEB's server copies events into shared memory; clients on the same machine read them and may skip events.
nodes.prose:
The MEB (monitoring event builder) serves built events through `XtcMonitorServer`, under a tag that clients use to find it. A transition is copied into a transition buffer, and its index is sent to every ready client. An L1Accept is queued for a task thread that copies it into an event buffer: a free one or, if none is free, one taken back from a client's queue. With neither, the L1Accept is dropped.

A client, for example a psana script with `DataSource(shmem=tag)`, connects to the shared memory on the same machine. In psana, the background reader keeps every transition but holds at most one L1Accept, and takes no new L1Accept until the analysis has used it. Meanwhile the server takes back the buffers of events that wait in the client's queue, so a client that is slower than the data skips events. No event building happens in psana in this mode; the server already delivers built events.

code_refs.note: events(): an L1Accept goes to _send and is Deferred; a transition is copied into a transition buffer and sent to every ready client.
_send: a free buffer from the request queue or, failing that, one taken from a client's output queue (NO_STEAL is not defined); with neither, the event is dropped.
psana's reader thread queues transitions and holds one L1Accept; while it holds one it asks only for transitions, until __next__ releases the hold.

nodes.title: AMI: online analysis
nodes.summary: AMI workers read the MEB's shared memory and feed a graphical analysis graph that operators and users build.
nodes.prose:
AMI is the graphical online-analysis program used with the LCLS-II DAQ (data acquisition system). The public AMI page describes building an analysis graph from data-source, operation and display boxes, and running it either on recorded files or live.

In a hutch configuration file such as `tmo.cnf`, each AMI worker node runs its own MEB (monitoring event builder) and an `ami-node` worker process that reads `psana://shmem=<hutch>`, together with `ami-manager`, `ami-global` and `ami-client` processes. The public page on AMI latency notes that when event processing is very slow, AMI pushes back into the MEB's shared-memory buffers, which adds latency.

code_refs.note: AMI processes in a hutch configuration; one MEB per AMI worker node.

nodes.title: Run control
nodes.summary: One control process runs the DAQ state machine, sends transitions to all processes, and starts runs in the logbook.
nodes.prose:
One control process drives a DAQ (data acquisition system) platform: a set of DRP (data reduction pipeline), TEB (trigger event builder) and MEB (monitoring event builder) processes listed in a `.cnf` file. It runs a state machine, sends transitions to the other processes over ZeroMQ (a messaging library), collects their replies, and inserts the corresponding timing transitions through the XPM (eXperiment Partition Master). Operators drive it from the control GUI (graphical user interface), the `daqstate` command or Python scripts built on `DaqControl`.

At Configure the trigger configuration is fetched from the configuration database. At BeginRun, if recording is enabled, a run number is allocated and the run is recorded in the logbook.

decisions.title: Two-phase transitions
decisions.decision: Configure, Unconfigure, BeginRun, EndRun, BeginStep, EndStep, Enable and Disable each have two phases (Disconnect is a single exchange, and SlowUpdate is only inserted into the timing stream). In phase 1 the control process publishes the transition over ZeroMQ and waits for the DRP, TEB and MEB processes to answer; slow work such as configuring a detector happens here. In phase 2 it inserts the transition into the timing stream through the XPM and waits for the phase-2 answers; only after Enable's phase 2 does it turn triggers on.
decisions.rationale: The internal Two Phase Transitions page gives the reasons. The phase-1 broadcast lets slow steps such as configuring run in parallel on all nodes. As much work as possible is done in phase 1, so that phase 2, in the DRP thread that handles the timing stream, stays quick. All timeouts are kept in the control level.

code_refs.note: condition_enable: phase 1, insert Enable, phase-2 replies, then enable triggers.
SlowUpdate: no phase 1 and no phase-2 replies; only inserted through the XPM.
Disconnect: one published message and one round of replies.

nodes.title: Control process and state machine
nodes.summary: control.py's CollectionManager walks the states from unallocated to running and back, one transition at a time.
nodes.prose:
The control process (`control`, class `CollectionManager` in `control.py`) runs a state machine whose states lead from `reset` through `unallocated`, `allocated`, `connected`, `configured`, `starting` and `paused` to `running`. Each step up has its own transition (`rollcall`, `alloc`, `connect`, `configure`, `beginrun`, `beginstep`, `enable`), and `dealloc`, `disconnect`, `unconfigure`, `endrun`, `endstep` and `disable` each lead one step back down; `reset` returns to `reset` from any state, and `slowupdate` is allowed in `running` without a state change.

Rollcall asks every process of the platform (the processes the control process drives) to answer, to learn which are running; alloc chooses among those that answered; connect has them set up their connections. A client can ask for a target state, and the control process walks the needed transitions one by one.

At BeginRun with recording on, the control process gets a run number by starting a run in the logbook and sends it, with a monitor-only flag for each detector, to the DRPs (data reduction pipelines) in the BeginRun message.

code_refs.note: The state machine.
Rollcall: publish rollcall on 'all' every second until every expected process has answered or the time-out expires.
condition_beginrun: run number and per-detector monitor flags for phase 1.

nodes.dev_notes: Without recording, the run number is 0 by convention.

nodes.title: Collection: how processes take part
nodes.summary: Every DRP, TEB and MEB is a CollectionApp: it receives transitions on ZeroMQ and sends its answers back.
nodes.prose:
Every process that the control process drives, each DRP (data reduction pipeline), TEB (trigger event builder) and MEB (monitoring event builder), is built on `CollectionApp`. It subscribes to the control process's ZeroMQ (a messaging library) PUB (publish) socket on the `all` topic and, after alloc, also on `partition`, and sends replies to the control process's PULL socket, which collects messages from many senders. The ports are a base port (29980) plus the platform number (the `-p` number of the DAQ instance) plus a fixed offset. Messages are JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) dictionaries with a header (key, message ID, sender ID) and a body; keys such as `configure`, `beginrun` or `enable` go to `handlePhase1`, the handler for phase 1 of a transition ([[control]]).

A second, in-process channel lets the process's own threads send messages out. A `pulseId` message from one of these threads is forwarded to the control process as a `timingTransition` reply whose message ID is the pulse ID; file reports, error messages and chunk requests are passed on under their own keys.

code_refs.note: The CollectionApp loop: ZeroMQ messages to handlers, in-process messages to the control process.

nodes.title: Configuration database
nodes.summary: Detector and trigger settings are typed JSON documents in a database, looked up by instrument, alias and device.
nodes.prose:
Detector and trigger settings live in a configuration database. The internal ConfigDB page describes it as a MongoDB database whose documents are typed JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): the values plus a `:types:` entry giving each value's type. It is reached at a URL that the control process passes to the other processes in the connect message.

At Configure the control process fetches the trigger configuration for its configuration alias (for example `BEAM`). Detector code uses `get_config()`, which returns the settings of `<detector>_<segment>` for an alias, using the instrument and database named in the connect message. The operator page adds that edits to the database take effect only at the next Configure: operators step the DAQ (data acquisition system) back down to Connected and then configure it again.

code_refs.note: How a detector's settings are looked up.

nodes.title: Launching: procmgr and .cnf files
nodes.summary: A hutch's .cnf file lists the processes of a platform with their command lines; procmgr starts and stops them.
nodes.prose:
The processes of a platform (one DAQ instance: a control process and the processes it drives) are listed in a `.cnf` file, a small Python script per hutch, for example `tmo.cnf`. Each entry gives a unique ID and a command line, and optionally a host (the default is the local machine) and flags. The command lines are built from shared option strings such as the instrument (`-P`), the collection host (`-C`) and, for DRPs (data reduction pipelines), the output directory (`-o`) and device (`-d`).

`procmgr` starts, stops, restarts and reports on them (`procmgr start | stop | stopall | restart | status <cnf>`); the `u` and `p` flags make it add `-u <id>` and `-p <platform>`. Processes that control the XPM (eXperiment Partition Master) boards are kept in a separate, long-lived `.cnf` file and are not stopped by a plain `stop`. A launcher based on Slurm (a cluster job scheduler), `daqmgr`, is an alternative.

code_refs.note: Shared options and the teb, monReqServer and drp command lines.
A procmgr_config entry needs cmd and id; host (default localhost) and flags are optional.

nodes.title: After the run
nodes.summary: Facility services outside this repository move files to storage; psana reads the small data, joins the streams by timestamp and fetches big data by offset.
nodes.prose:
Moving the files that the DAQ (data acquisition system) wrote is a facility mechanism outside this repository. Per the public smalldata_tools debugging page and the internal Live Mode page, services called data movers, also outside this repository, carry each run's files from the recording machines to the storage system; a file still in transit has an extra `.inprogress` suffix ([[data-movement]]). Analysis then reads the files with psana.

psana finds the run's streams, reads the small-data files first, and builds each event by matching timestamps across the streams: an L1Accept may be present in some streams and missing from others, but every transition must be present in all of them. It then reads only the bytes it needs from the big-data files, using the offsets stored in the small data. The same files can also be read while the run is still being recorded (live mode).

code_refs.note: Joining the streams by timestamp.

decisions.title: Read the small data first, the big data by offset
decisions.decision: psana does not scan the big-data files. It reads the small-data files of all streams, builds the events from them, and then reads only the needed bytes of the big-data files, using the stored offsets and sizes.
decisions.rationale: The internal XTC for LCLS-II page gives the purpose of the small-data files: one small event per big event, used to parallelize the reading and, when small values are added, to filter events before paying for the large data. The public parallel-analysis page shows the parallel use: one rank reads the small data and sends batches on, and big-data ranks read the full events.

nodes.title: Moving files to storage
nodes.summary: Data movers, a facility service outside this repository, transfer each run's files from the DAQ machines to storage.
nodes.prose:
Moving the files from the recording nodes to storage is done by facility services. The public smalldata_tools debugging page names the data movers as the services that transfer the data from the machines that record it to the storage system, and says that when psana waits in vain for a run's files, the movers are usually the problem.

The internal Live Mode page adds that a mover gives an `.xtc2` file an extra `.inprogress` extension while the file is being moved, which lets users see when moving is complete. The same page discusses how this interacts with reading files while they are still growing, and notes that because the small-data files are not chunked, chunking does not complicate live reading.

nodes.title: psana: finding and reading a run
nodes.summary: psana finds one small-data file per stream, matches each with its big-data file, and splits the work across MPI ranks.
nodes.prose:
With `DataSource(exp=..., run=...)`, psana reads from the experiment's `xtc` directory, by default `$SIT_PSDM_DATA/<exp[:3]>/<exp>/xtc`, which holds the files in the layout described under [[files]]. It asks the logbook's database for the run's file list and expects one small-data file per stream in `xtc/smalldata`; outside live mode, if no list is available, it scans that directory for `*r<run>-s*.smd.xtc2` files. Every small-data file must have a matching big-data file, and in live mode files still named `.inprogress` are accepted.

Under MPI (Message Passing Interface), one rank reads the small data, event-builder ranks build batches of events, and big-data ranks read the full events and run the user's event loop.

code_refs.note: Finding the small-data files and their big-data partners.
A `.inprogress` file is returned under its own name only from the retry loop, which runs only when max_retries > 0 (in live mode, line 229).

nodes.title: Joining the streams by timestamp
nodes.summary: psana's event builder takes the smallest next timestamp across all streams and joins the datagrams that share it.
nodes.prose:
psana's event builder (`eventbuilder.pyx`) builds events from the small-data streams. At each step it looks at the next datagram of every stream and takes the smallest timestamp; every stream whose next datagram has that same timestamp contributes to the event, and the other streams keep their datagram for a later event. An L1Accept can therefore be present in only some streams, for example from detectors in a slower readout group.

A transition, however, must be present in all streams: if it is not, psana raises an error that names the transition and the number of streams it expected and received. The internal SlowUpdate Handling page records this requirement as a constraint on the DAQ (data acquisition system).

code_refs.note: _gather_event: smallest timestamp, matching streams, complete transitions.

tour.title: Follow one L1Accept from the pulse to psana
tour.intro: This tour follows one L1Accept, the readout of a single accelerator pulse, from the timing system through the DAQ (data acquisition system) to the files, live monitoring and psana. The first step sets the scene: before any event is read out, the control process has configured the system, begun a run and enabled triggers. Each later step zooms the map to the component it is about, highlights the flows involved and says what happens to our event there; the component's own description follows the step text.

steps.title: Before the event: Configure, BeginRun, BeginStep, then Enable turns on triggers
steps.prose: This step sets the scene before our event exists. The control process steps the platform, the DRP (data reduction pipeline), TEB (trigger event builder) and MEB (monitoring event builder) processes it drives, from Connected to Running through four transitions in this order: Configure (Connected to Configured), BeginRun (Configured to Starting), BeginStep (Starting to Paused) and Enable (Paused to Running). These transitions go first to the processes over ZeroMQ (a messaging library), then into the timing stream through the XPM (eXperiment Partition Master). At Configure the TEB loads its trigger plugin; at BeginRun with recording on, a run number is allocated and each recording DRP begins its files with Configure and BeginRun. Enable turns on the XPM's triggers, so per-pulse events, the L1Accepts, can flow.

code_refs.note: The state machine: which transition leads to which state.
At BeginRun the cached Configure is written first.

steps.title: The accelerator pulse and its pulse ID
steps.prose: Our event begins as one accelerator bucket, one of the 910,000 time slots that the accelerator provides every 0.98 seconds, that is at about 929 kHz. The timing frame for that bucket carries its event codes, which arrive about 100 microseconds before the beam, and its beam destination. Every readout of this pulse that a DRP (data reduction pipeline) receives by DMA (direct memory access) will carry a timing header whose first word holds the pulse ID in its low 56 bits, followed by the timestamp.

code_refs.note: PulseId and TimingHeader.

steps.title: The XPM triggers the readout group
steps.prose: All detectors of a readout group share one trigger selection (an event code, a fixed or AC (alternating-current) power-line rate, or a sequence). So the XPM (eXperiment Partition Master) decides in its firmware, outside this repository, whether this pulse triggers each readout group; that decision is the L0 trigger. The readout groups that triggered travel with the pulse's timing information; in our event's timing header they are the low 16 bits of the `env` word ([[pulse-id]]). An event without the platform's common readout group is discarded early in the DRP (data reduction pipeline) and counted.

code_refs.note: The readout groups are the low 16 bits of env.
The XPM firmware registers of the L0 trigger.
The per-group trigger selection modes.

steps.title: The front-end reads out and sends the data over PGP
steps.prose: In the detector's readout firmware, which is outside this repository, a timing-receiver module turns the timing stream into an in-time trigger decision and the event's timing information. The detector reads out, and its data travel over a PGP link, one of the serial readout links of the DAQ (data acquisition system), to a DRP (data reduction pipeline) node. There the readout card's firmware, also outside this repository, writes them, together with the timing header, into a DMA (direct memory access) buffer in memory.

steps.title: The DRP reads the DMA buffers and checks the timing header
steps.prose: The PGP reader of the DRP (data reduction pipeline) collects the completed DMA (direct memory access) buffers and asks the detector class where each buffer's timing header is. The event counter in that header picks our event's slot, and the event is complete when every PGP lane (serial readout link) of the detector has delivered its buffer. The reader checks that the event counter advanced by one since the last complete event. Events that lack the common readout group are discarded at this point and counted.

code_refs.note: Timing header, event slot, completion and the event-counter check.
Events without the common readout group are discarded and counted (m_nNoComRoG).

steps.title: A worker builds the XTC2 datagram with the detector class
steps.prose: A worker thread of the DRP (data reduction pipeline) takes our event and calls the detector class's `event()` method. The method writes the event's values into an XTC2 datagram (the DAQ's self-describing data record) with `CreateData`, against the `Names` that the class declared in the Configure datagram. The datagram is built in our event's slot of the pebble, the DRP's large buffer for datagrams.

steps.title: The trigger input goes to the TEB
steps.prose: Besides the datagram, the DRP (data reduction pipeline) prepares a small trigger contribution for the TEB (trigger event builder): the datagram header plus a few bytes from its trigger-primitive plugin (compiled code loaded from a shared library). The collector thread hands it to the `TebContributor`, which sends it to the TEB in a batch with neighbouring pulse IDs. The detector data of our event stay in the DRP.

steps.title: The TEB builds the event by pulse ID and the trigger plugin decides
steps.prose: The TEB (trigger event builder) collects the contributions with our event's pulse ID from the DRPs (data reduction pipelines) that provide trigger input. Once every expected contributor has arrived, the event is passed on in pulse ID order to the trigger plugin, which fills in the result: `persist` to record the event and `monitor` to send it to live monitoring; the TEB itself adds `prescale` from the event's `keepRaw` bit. If a contribution is missing, the event is forced out, at the latest after a time-out, and marked as damaged.

code_refs.note: process(): each contribution goes into the event with its pulse ID; a complete event becomes due and events up to it are flushed in order.
_flush: an older incomplete event is fixed up when a newer complete event has the same contract; otherwise only after the time-out.

steps.title: The result returns and each DRP acts on it
steps.prose: The TEB (trigger event builder) sends the result, a `ResultDgram`, back to the DRPs (data reduction pipelines) in the event's readout groups. Each DRP's result receiver finds our waiting event by its buffer index and checks that the pulse ID matches. Because recording is on, it writes the event if `persist` or `prescale` is set; if `monitor` is set and the result names an MEB (monitoring event builder) buffer, it also sends the event there.

code_refs.note: TebReceiver::complete: write, monitor, acknowledge.

steps.title: The event is appended to the .xtc2 big-data file
steps.prose: Our event was accepted, so each DRP (data reduction pipeline) that read it out and is recording appends its datagram to its own big-data file, `<exp>-r<run>-s<stream>-c<chunk>.xtc2`, through a buffered writer whose own thread writes full buffers to disk. Our event goes into whichever chunk file is open; new chunks start at an Enable ([[chunking]]). The pieces of the event now sit in several files, one for each recording DRP that read the event out.

code_refs.note: The buffered writer with its writer thread.
A monitor-only DRP sets run_number to 0 and opens no files; files are opened only when recording.

steps.title: The .smd.xtc2 file records where the event is
steps.prose: For the same datagram the DRP (data reduction pipeline) appends a small record to its small-data file, `smalldata/<exp>-r<run>-s<stream>-c000.smd.xtc2`. The record is a datagram with our event's timestamp and `env` word whose payload is only the event's offset in the current big-data chunk and its size in bytes. psana will read these small records first.

code_refs.note: Smd::generate: for an L1Accept, a datagram with the time, env and the values intOffset and intDgramSize.
Each written datagram goes to both files.

steps.title: If asked, a copy goes to live monitoring
steps.prose: If the result asked for monitoring and an MEB (monitoring event builder) had offered a free buffer, every DRP (data reduction pipeline) writes its part of our event directly into that buffer with RDMA (remote direct memory access). The MEB builds the parts into one event by pulse ID and serves it in shared memory, where AMI or a psana script on that machine may see it; a client slower than the data may skip it. If no buffer was free, our event is recorded but not monitored.

code_refs.note: The DRP side: post the event into the chosen MEB buffer.
The post is an RDMA write (writedata) into the MEB's memory.

steps.title: After the run the files are moved to storage
steps.prose: Our event's files leave the machines that recorded them through a facility mechanism that is not part of this repository: data movers copy them to the storage system, and a file still in transit carries an extra `.inprogress` suffix. For some instruments the files are written to the FFB (fast-feedback) file system first, where analysis can read them while the experiment runs.

steps.title: psana joins the streams and reads the event back
steps.prose: psana reads the small-data file of every stream of the run. Its event builder takes the smallest next timestamp across the streams: the small records of our event, one from each DRP (data reduction pipeline) that recorded it, share that timestamp and are joined into one event. Only then does psana read our event's bytes from each big-data file, using the stored offsets and sizes. This is the first place where the recorded parts of our event come together.

code_refs.note: _gather_event: smallest timestamp, matching streams.
